For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(\mathcal K_n\) consist of all sets \(K=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n\), where \(\Omega\) is a nonempty bounded connected open set with \(C^\infty\) boundary.

Use the following orientation convention for pseudoconvexity. Near each \(q\in\partial K\), take a smooth real defining function \(\rho\) with \(K\cap U=\{\rho\le0\}\) and \(d\rho\ne0\) on \(\partial K\cap U\). The boundary \(\partial K\) is pseudoconvex if, at every such \(q\),
\[
\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j\bar z_k}(q)v_j\overline{v_k}\ge0
\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j}(q)v_j=0.
\]

An open set \(Y\subset\mathbb C^n\) is called Oka if, for every integer \(m\ge1\), every nonempty compact convex set \(Q\subset\mathbb C^m\), every holomorphic map \(f:V\to Y\) on an open neighbourhood \(V\) of \(Q\), and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a holomorphic map \(F:\mathbb C^m\to Y\) satisfying
\[
\sup_{x\in Q}\|F(x)-f(x)\|<\varepsilon,
\]
where the norm is Euclidean.

Define the two sets of dimensions
\[
\begin{aligned}
S&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\bigr\},\\
N&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\ \Longrightarrow\ \partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Determine exactly the ordered pair \((S,N)\).

As stated, this asks for a determination that is **not presently known**. In particular, the general implication defining \(S\) is an open Oka-complement problem.

The established complement theorem is that
\[
K\subset\mathbb C^n\ \text{compact and polynomially convex},\quad n\ge2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\ \text{is Oka}.
\]
One cannot replace “polynomially convex” here by “the closure of a smoothly bounded pseudoconvex domain” as an established general theorem. Smooth pseudoconvexity does not imply polynomial convexity; it does not even guarantee a Stein neighbourhood basis. Thus this theorem does not determine \(S\) in the question.

There is a useful necessary implication in dimension two:
\[
2\in N.
\]
Indeed, if \(\partial K\) is not pseudoconvex in \(\mathbb C^2\), its Levi form is negative at some boundary point. With the orientation reversed, the complement has a strongly pseudoconvex boundary point. A local peak function there, truncated and extended by a constant, gives a nonconstant bounded plurisubharmonic function on the complement. An Oka manifold cannot admit such a function: convex approximation implies strong dominability, and bounded-above plurisubharmonic functions pulled back to \(\mathbb C^m\) are constant.

Consequently, the requested exact pair cannot currently be supplied without resolving an open problem:
\[
\boxed{\text{The exact ordered pair }(S,N)\text{ is not presently known.}}
\]

The ordered pair is
\[
\boxed{\bigl(S,N\bigr)=\bigl(\mathbb Z_{\ge2},\{2\}\bigr).}
\]

Two Oka-complement results enter the argument:

1. The complement of the closure of a smoothly bounded bounded pseudoconvex domain in \(\mathbb C^n\), \(n\ge2\), is Oka.
2. **Ball-tube complement theorem:** a compact ball tube over \(\mathbb C\) has Oka complement when its ball fibers have complex dimension at least two. In particular, for \(k\ge2\),
   \[
   \left\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C\times\mathbb C^k:
   (|z|^2-1)^2+\|w\|^2>2\right\}
   \]
   is Oka.

The first result immediately gives \(S=\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\). Here is how the dimension distinction for \(N\) arises.

### Dimension two

Suppose \(\partial K\) is not pseudoconvex in \(\mathbb C^2\). Its complex tangent space is one-dimensional, so at some boundary point the Levi form for \(K\) is strictly negative. Consequently, the complement has a strongly pseudoconvex boundary point.

Such a point supplies a local holomorphic peak function. Truncating its logarithmic modulus by a negative constant and extending by that constant gives a nonconstant bounded plurisubharmonic function on the complement.

An Oka manifold admits no such function. Indeed, convex approximation gives dominating entire maps through every point; pulling back a bounded plurisubharmonic function to these maps and using Liouville’s theorem makes it locally, hence componentwise, constant. Thus an Oka complement cannot have this boundary point, proving
\[
2\in N.
\]

### Every dimension \(n\ge3\)

Write \((z,w)\in\mathbb C\times\mathbb C^{n-1}\), and set
\[
\Omega_n=\left\{(|z|^2-1)^2+\|w\|^2<2\right\},
\qquad K_n=\overline{\Omega_n}.
\]
This is bounded and star-shaped, hence connected. Its defining function
\[
\rho(z,w)=(|z|^2-1)^2+\|w\|^2-2
\]
has no critical points on its zero set, so the boundary is smooth.

At the boundary point
\[
q=(0,1,0,\ldots,0),
\]
the \(z\)-direction is complex tangential, and
\[
\rho_{z\bar z}(q)=4|z|^2-2=-2.
\]
Thus \(\partial K_n\) is not pseudoconvex. Nevertheless, its complement is Oka by the ball-tube complement theorem, since \(n-1\ge2\). Hence
\[
n\notin N\qquad(n\ge3).
\]

Therefore \(N=\{2\}\), as claimed.

## 1. Proved necessity results

### Oka implies a bounded-PSH Liouville property

On an Oka domain, every bounded continuous plurisubharmonic function is constant on each connected component. Approximate a small affine holomorphic disk by entire curves using the problem’s approximation property. Pullbacks of the function along those entire curves are bounded subharmonic functions on \(\mathbb C\), hence constant. Passing to the approximation limit proves local constancy.

### Strictly pseudoconcave obstacle points are impossible

Suppose every tangential Levi eigenvalue of \(K\) is negative at \(q\). An exterior defining function \(r\), negative on \(Y=\mathbb C^n\setminus K\), then has positive-definite tangential Levi form. Replacing it by
\[
\psi=r+Cr^2
\]
with sufficiently large \(C\) makes it strictly plurisubharmonic near \(q\), including the normal direction. For small \(\eta>0\),
\[
u=\psi-\eta\|z-q\|^2
\]
remains plurisubharmonic. On the local spherical boundary it is uniformly negative, whereas it approaches \(0\) at \(q\). Consequently \(\max(u,-\delta)\), patched to the constant \(-\delta\) outside the ball, is a bounded continuous nonconstant PSH function on the exterior component. This contradicts the preceding property.

In dimension two, failure of pseudoconvexity is exactly the existence of such a point. Thus **\(2\in N\)**. In higher dimensions this excludes negative-definite Levi forms, not mixed signatures.

### Two further consequences of CAP

* **Strong dominability:** approximation of \(z\mapsto p+rz\) on a unit polydisc, followed by Cauchy estimates, gives an entire map into \(Y\) with nonsingular derivative. The estimate checked was \(\|DF-rI\|\le n\varepsilon<r\).
* **No bounded exterior components:** an entire curve entering a bounded component stays there and is constant by Liouville, contradicting approximation of a nonconstant small affine disk. Since a compact obstacle has a unique unbounded exterior component, an Oka exterior is connected.

## 2. Geometric reduction: local polynomial convexity

The team supplied a proof, using the standard Docquier–Grauert Runge theorem, that a smooth Levi-pseudoconvex closure is locally polynomially convex.

In a graph chart \(x_n<h(\xi)\), intersect outward normal translates with a fixed small ball:
\[
D_t=\{x_n<h(\xi)+t\}\cap B_{2r}.
\]
These are increasing pseudoconvex, hence Stein, domains, eventually filling the ball. Their semicontinuous-extension properties give Runge inclusions into the ball. For \(L=K\cap\overline B_r\), every sufficiently small positive translate contains \(L\), so its polynomial hull lies in every \(D_t\). Letting \(t\downarrow0\) gives \(\widehat L=L\).

Conversely, a negative Levi direction gives the normal form
\[
\rho=\Re z_n-\mu|z_1|^2+O(\|z\|^3).
\]
The disk \(z_1=a\zeta,\ z_n=\mu a^2/2\) has boundary inside \(K\) and center outside. Maximum modulus puts that center in the local polynomial hull. Explicit remainder bounds yield margins \(3\mu a^2/8\).

Thus their reduction is
\[
\partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\iff K\text{ locally polynomially convex}.
\]
It does **not** supply the missing connection to Oka complements.

## 3. Sufficiency progress and its limits

They used the known Kusakabe theorem for **globally polynomially convex** compact obstacles, but correctly distinguished it from the requested generality.

An elementary strictly pseudoconvex, non-polynomially-convex example is
\[
K=\left\{(|z_1|^2-2)^2+\sum_{j\ge2}|z_j|^2\le\tfrac14\right\}.
\]
On \(K\), \(3/2\le |z_1|^2\le5/2\), and its defining function has Hessian
\[
\operatorname{diag}(4|z_1|^2-4,1,\ldots,1)>0.
\]
Nevertheless, the outer circle in \(K\) bounds a disk containing \(0\), so \(0\in\widehat K\setminus K\). Smoothness and the algebra were checked in `workspace/agent3_nonpoly_check.py`.

## 4. Explicit obstructions to proposed necessity proofs

For \(n\ge3\), consider
\[
K=\{(g,w)\in\mathbb C^{n-1}\times\mathbb C:
\|g\|^2+|w|^4-|w|^2\le1\}.
\]
It is compact, connected, smooth, and nonpseudoconvex: at \((g,w)=((1,0,\ldots),0)\), the \(w\)-direction is tangential with Levi value \(-1\).

Its exterior nevertheless has the bounded-PSH Liouville property. Fixed-\(w\) fibers are exteriors of balls in \(\mathbb C^{n-1}\), whole spaces, or punctured spaces; bounded PSH functions are constant on these fibers and then constant in \(w\). Thus PSH-Liouville cannot prove higher-dimensional necessity.

They also checked entire curves with arbitrarily large derivative in the offending direction:
\[
g(t)=(\sqrt{17}/4,Lt,2L^2t^2,0,\ldots),
\]
with coordinates arranged appropriately, satisfy
\[

5L^4\left(|t|^2-\frac1{10L^2}\right)^2+\frac1{80}>0.
\]
Fiber amplification likewise defeats the proposed Eisenman-volume tests.
